definition: The heuristic-systematic model is a cognition framework that views judgments and decisions as being shaped by two kinds of processing: more effortful, systematic thinking and more shortcut-based, heuristic responding. In the source context, it is used to explain how information overload can hinder systematic thought and shift people’s purchase decisions.

reasons: The packet does not define the heuristic-systematic model as a two-process framework with “systematic” versus “heuristic” processing; that theory-level description is not supported by the supplied text.

The claim that the model explains judgments and decisions generally is broader than the packet, which only says the article uses the model as a perspective for studying information overload in live commerce.

The statement about information overload hindering systematic thought and shifting purchase decisions is only partially supported: the packet says information overload can make consumers think systematically less easily and affect purchase decisions, but it does not substantiate the broader causal framing in the definition.
The packet does not define the “heuristic-systematic model” as involving “two kinds of processing” (systematic vs heuristic) or describe them as “more effortful” vs “shortcut-based.”

The packet only states that the study “introduces information overload from the perspective of ‘Heuristic-systematic model’” and that information overload makes it “difficult for consumers to think systematically,” without stating any broader model mechanism about heuristic responding.
